newsitem.title: USA: G7 ministers provide little forex market fodder.
newsitem.headline: G7 ministers provide little forex market fodder.

text.p: Currency traders hoping for some business-boosting market volatility are likely to get little joy from this weekend's meetings by finance ministers and central bankers from major industrial nations.

Finance and monetary officials from the Group of Seven nations touched on a broad range of issues, including debt relief for poor countries, Europe's plans for a single currency and the need to avoid complacency over inflation.
But they went out of their way to avoid rattling the comfortable stability of currency markets in recent months.

"The (currency) market was expecting very neutral G7 statements and it appears that that's what they got," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan. "When all is said and done, there's not much there for the markets to sink their teeth into."

The G7 "welcomed developments in exchange markets over the recent period" and reaffirmed its commitment to "cooperate closely" on the exchange rate front, in a statement by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin after Saturday meetings ended.

Finance ministers from other G7 nations echoed Rubin's statement and stressed the need for a strong dollar. They fell short of arguing for a further strengthening in the greenback from current levels.
Analysts noted that France did not call for a stronger dollar, as some had expected. This could do some modest damage to the U.S. currency's recent gains versus Europe, they said.
The dollar posted ample gains last week despite the Federal Reserve's decision to keep short-term U.S. interest rates unchanged. It closed at around 1.5240 marks on Friday.

"The fact that (French Finance Minister Jean) Arthuis has not called for a stronger dollar does not give us much fuel for an extension of the dollar rally," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.

However, Finstrom said any weakness versus European currencies would likely be fleeting and predicted some dollar strength versus the yen on the heels of ostensibly conciliatory talks between the U.S. and Japan.
After the G7 meeting on Saturday, Rubin said Japan seemed committed to policies to keep its economy growing.
"I certainly came away satisfied," Rubin said. "They are very focused on the importance of having an appropriate mix of fiscal and monetary policies to maintain growth."
Analysts had expected harsher rhetoric from the U.S. in pushing Japan to stimulate its economy. A stronger Japanese economy would boost U.S. exports to Japan, easing the bilateral trade deficit.

Economists said Rubin's comments suggested that Japan is a long way away from raising interest rates, which would support the dollar versus the yen. But on the whole, they expected only modest exchange rate movements to result from the talks.
"What we've seen from the G7 reflects the fact that they don't want to do anything to rattle currency markets," said Robert Hormats, vice chairman at Goldman Sachs(International).

"The U.S. doesn't want the dollar to go up a lot, because then they'll get more angry letters from Detroit (auto manufacturers) and they don't want it to get down because it would adversely affect the U.S. bond market," he said.
Hormats also downplayed suggestions that discussion of Europe's single currency plans will take on a more prominent role at future G7 meetings.
"At this point the debate is really a very European debate," he said. "I think it doesn't help for the G7 to take it up because they're not going to add much."
